catalog_quote: 4. Foot. Every morpheme that consists of more than one syllable has one predictable stress. Morphemes that consist only of one or two consonants do not have stress. Stress falls on the final syllable of a morpheme that has at least one vowel unless that syllable is V or CV, in which case stress falls on the penultimate syllable; if there is no penultimate syllable, a V or CV morpheme is not stressed. A foot consists of from one to eight (and possibly more) morphemes, including those that carry stress and those that do not. Epenthetic vowels are added according to rule, as outlined below in the section on morphophonemics, in order to shape the string of morphemes into permitted syllable patterns. new_statements.quote: p. 62: "Por fim, consideremos ainda o par [k]/[g] nas palavras [akaj] "fruta" e [pigaɾ] "tu, te, ti, você", em que esses dois segmentos aparecem em contextos idênticos: sílaba tônica de final de palavra, iniciando sílaba pesada cuja rima começa pela vogal [a]:" || p. 103-104: "Um exemplo de síncope pode ser observado na elocução [oskãntãn] "ela sentou-se", cuja estrutura abstrata é /usakãntãn/ [...] tem características de uma regra fonética, pós-lexical, com atuação em sílabas átonas de palavras com mais de duas sílabas, de forma idêntica ao que observou Bisol (1993: 10) em relação à maioria das vogais do português."
new_statements.translation: p. 62: "Finally, let us also consider the pair [k]/[g] in the words [akaj] 'fruit' and [pigaɾ] 'you (sg.)', in which these two segments appear in identical contexts: the word-final stressed (tonic) syllable, beginning a heavy syllable whose rhyme starts with the vowel [a]:" || p. 103-104: "An example of syncope can be seen in the utterance [oskãntãn] 'she sat down', whose abstract structure is /usakãntãn/ [...] it has the characteristics of a phonetic, post-lexical rule operating in unstressed (atonic) syllables of words with more than two syllables, exactly as Bisol (1993: 10) observed for most vowels of Portuguese."

new_statements.relation_note: The catalog record for Wapishana has an empty rule and there are no existing statements; this work adds only incidental evidence (word stress exists; word-final tonic syllable in [a'kaj] and [pi'gaɾ], both with closed final syllables; syncope targets unstressed syllables in words of 3+ syllables) and no placement rule, so it neither confirms nor contradicts anything recorded. Describes the Brazilian (Roraima: Malacacheta and Pium malocas) variety, not the Guyanese variety described by Tracy (1972), which it summarizes without any stress statement.
new_statements.rule_in_words: No stress rule is stated anywhere in the dissertation; it is a segmental and syllable-structure study (CV theory) of Brazilian Wapishana and has no suprasegmental/accent section (table of contents checked; searches for acento, tônic-, áton-, acentu-, proemin-, pé, ritmo, prosód- run over the whole text). The only usable statements are incidental: (a) the language has tonic vs. atonic syllables; (b) in the disyllables [a.'kaj] 'fruit' and [pi.'gaɾ] 'you' the tonic syllable is the word-final (closed, 'heavy') syllable; (c) an optional post-lexical syncope deletes a weak vowel in unstressed syllables of words of more than two syllables, the example being the second syllable of four-syllable /usakãntãn/ -> [oskãntãn]. Transcriptions in the text and in the appendix wordlist (pp. 116-119) do not mark stress; the accents the scanned shows on vowels are nasalization tildes (verified on the page scan). Two disyllables with final stress on a closed syllable are consistent with either final stress or weight-sensitive stress, but the work does not decide.
new_statements.identity_note: Santos 1995 describes the Wapishana spoken on the Brazilian side (Roraima: Malacacheta maloca, 36 km SE of Boa Vista, and Pium maloca on the Tacutu river), from five male speakers; it contrasts this with the Guyanese variety of Tracy (1972) and concludes that segmental differences exist but syllable structure is identical. No stress statement is attributed to Tracy in the summary.

(2) Deciding source is a 1972 7-page SIL phonology sketch, but the best available description (Santos 2006 UNICAMP doctoral grammar, held under our earlier reading) has a full stress section (2.4, pp.76-87) that confirms every coded field: weight-sensitive, right-edge, final syllable stressed iff heavy (CVC, CVV long, CVG, VC) else penult, analysed as L-to-R iambs with End Rule right; it adds that final light vowels are normally devoiced or deleted so surface words end in a stressed heavy syllable, and iambic lengthening repairs light-light words. tone.quote: Unstressed vowels in spoken Wapishana are usually quiet or dropped altogether. [...] Wapishana always stresses the last syllable in a word that ends in a long vowel or a consonant. The word “makon” is stressed “maKON” since “KON” ends with the consonant “n”. But “mako” is stressed “MAko” since the final “ko” has only a short vowel. However, when long “ii”, “oo”, or “uu” vowels are stressed they turn into “ia”, “oa” or “ua” respectively.
